binders: For every natural number m, including m = 0, let I = {0,...,m-1} and V = I → ℝ, identified with ℝ^m.
For every function q : ℝ → ℝ → V; its first argument is the spatial variable and its second argument is the time variable in the formulas.
For every fixed matrix A = coefficient : I → I → ℝ.
For every pair of real numbers x and t.
For every vector v₀ = qx ∈ V supplied as a candidate spatial derivative.

Under the outer derivative hypothesis, the left side existentially binds a ∈ V and then b ∈ V. The right side independently existentially binds c ∈ V and then d ∈ V. These witnesses are chosen for the fixed outer data; there is no single witness required to work at all points.
hypotheses: The real-variable map ξ ↦ q(ξ,t) has derivative v₀ at ξ = x, using the usual real topology and the finite product topology on V.
conclusions: The following conditions are equivalent: (L) there exist a,b ∈ V such that τ ↦ q(x,τ) has derivative a at t, ξ ↦ A q(ξ,t) has derivative b at x, and a+b=0; (R) there exist c,d ∈ V such that τ ↦ q(x,τ) has derivative c at t, ξ ↦ q(ξ,t) has derivative d at x, and c+Ad=0.

Explicitly, the equation on the left is a_i+b_i=0 for every i∈I, and the equation on the right is c_i+Σ_{j∈I} A_ij d_j=0 for every i∈I. Each side requires both derivative assertions together with its equation.
mathematical_definitions: For v∈V, the flux F(v)=Av has coordinates F(v)_i=Σ_{j∈I} A_ij v_j. The same fixed matrix A is used at every argument of this flux.
Vector addition and scalar multiplication are pointwise, and 0∈V is the function i↦0. V carries the product of the usual real topologies.
For a map f:ℝ→V, having derivative v at s means f(s+h)=f(s)+hv+o(|h|) as h→0; equivalently, for every i∈I, the scalar coordinate function f_i has ordinary derivative v_i at s.
The spatial derivative holds t fixed; the time derivative holds x fixed. The derivative of the flux is the derivative of ξ↦F(q(ξ,t)), not a derivative with respect to the state variable.
The existential spatial derivative d on the right is not syntactically the outer vector v₀. Ordinary derivative uniqueness implies d=v₀ whenever its derivative assertion holds.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every nonnegative integer m, every real vector-valued function q of two real variables, every fixed real m-by-m matrix A, every real point (x,t), and every vector v₀, assume that q has spatial derivative v₀ at (x,t) with t held fixed. Then existence of a time derivative and a spatial derivative of the linear flux Aq whose sum is zero is equivalent to existence of a time derivative and a spatial derivative of q such that the time derivative plus A times the spatial derivative is zero. Each condition is asserted only at the chosen point, and explicitly includes existence of its stated derivatives.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The dimension is finite but need not be positive. When m=0, V has only the empty vector, all vector-valued maps involved are constant, and all coordinate equations are vacuous; the hypothesis and both sides hold.

The statement is conditional on existence of the specified spatial derivative of q. If that outer hypothesis fails for a supplied v₀, the implication places no requirement on the equivalence for that instance.
No time differentiability is assumed externally. If the time slice has no derivative at t, both existential conditions are false, so their equivalence can still hold.
A is an arbitrary fixed real square matrix. There is no invertibility, nondegeneracy, symmetry, spectral, or hyperbolicity assumption; the zero matrix is permitted.
The flux is exactly the homogeneous linear map v↦Av. The proposition does not quantify over arbitrary nonlinear fluxes or coefficients varying with space, time, or state.

All derivative assertions are at the selected point along full real-variable slices. No differentiability in a neighborhood, continuous derivatives, joint differentiability, or mixed derivatives are asserted.
Although x and t are universally quantified, the conclusion is a conditional equivalence at each chosen point. It does not assert that either equation holds throughout a region.
No initial or boundary conditions, integral conservation statement, weak or distributional formulation, solution existence theorem, or solution uniqueness theorem is encoded.
There is no domain restriction such as t≥0 or x lying in a spatial interval; q is defined on all of ℝ×ℝ.
